newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-BORIS BECKER URGED TO STAY IN GERMANY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BORIS BECKER URGED TO STAY IN GERMANY.

text.p: German tennis star Boris Becker's plans to move abroad in order to give his three-year old son a chance to lead a normal life were criticised on Wednesday by leading sports figures and politicians.

Becker said recently he wanted to move to the United States in about three years' time, when his son Noah started school so that the boy would avoid the enormous pressures in Germany of having a famous father and of not being white.

Becker said he and his wife, who is black, believed their son would be able to lead a more normal life in a multi-racial society. After tax investigators raided his Munich house last month, an angry Becker warned he could leave even sooner than that.
Franz Beckenbauer, once a legendary soccer star for Germany and now chairman of the Bayern Munich soccer team, and Bavarian Finance Minister Erwin Huber urged Becker to stay in Germany.

"You are not only an idol, but you have also become a role model," Beckenbauer told Bunte magazine. "You can't simply slip out of Germany just like that. You have a lot to do here after your days playing tennis are over."
Beckenbauer, who himself resides in nearby Austria to avoid high German taxes, once proposed that Becker, 29, become "Sport Minister" for Germany after he retires from tennis.
Huber appealed to Becker to stay in Germany rather than move to Miami, where the tennis star owns a house.
"Stay here Boris!" Huber said. "Your child is safer in Bavaria than in Florida."
Becker said in another interview with Der Spiegel magazine earlier this month he was also considering moving to New York, Paris or London before his son starts school.

In a December interview with SAT 1 television, Becker said he was proud to be German and liked living in Munich, but he enjoyed spending time in Florida because he could move about freely without protection from the fans who mob his every public appearance in Germany.

"The price I pay for my fame and success is my private life," Becker. "I can handle that for myself. But my son, it is not his fault he is my son. It is very unpleasant for me and my wife that he is so famous for no reason."
Bunte published an opinion poll showing that 86 percent of the people surveyed were opposed to the idea of giving top sports figures special tax treatment.
A number of high-income German sports figures have moved abroad in order to avoid high German taxes. Becker only returned to Germany in 1993 after living in Monaco for three years.
Steffi Graf, the world's number one woman tennis player, was a prominent exception to the exodus.
Her father Peter is currently on trial on charges that he evaded 19 million marks ($11.97 million) in taxes. A verdict is expected on January 24. ($1=1.5867 Mark)
